Multimodal Learning on Low-Quality Data with Conformal Predictive Self-Calibration     

Xun Jiang, Yufan Gu, Disen Hu, Yuqing Hou, Yazhou Yao, Fumin Shen, Heng Tao Shen, Xing Xu; Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2026, pp. 23041-23050

Abstract

Multimodal learning often grapples with the challenge of low-quality data, which predominantly manifests as two facets: modality imbalance and noisy corruption. While these issues are often studied in isolation, we argue that they share a common root in the predictive uncertainty towards the reliability of individual modalities and instances during learning. In this paper, we propose a unified framework, termed Conformal Predictive Self-Calibration (CPSC), which leverages conformal prediction to equip the model with the ability to perform self-guided calibration on-the-fly. The core of our proposed CPSC lies in a novel self-calibrating training loop that seamlessly integrates two key modules: (1) Representation Self-Calibration, which decomposes unimodal features into components, selectively fuses the most robust ones identified by a conformal predictor to enhance feature resilience. (2) Gradient Self-Calibration, which recalibrates the gradient flow during backpropagation based on instance-wise reliability scores, steering the optimization towards more trustworthy directions. Furthermore, we also devise a self-update strategy for the conformal predictor to ensure the entire system co-evolves consistently throughout the training process. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets under both imbalanced and noisy settings demonstrate that our CPSC framework consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunCHN/CPSC.

# Handling annotation uncertainty in human activity recognition

  * September 2019

DOI:10.1145/3341163.3347744


Developing systems for Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearables typically relies on datasets that were manually annotated by human experts with regards to precise timings of instances of relevant activities. However, obtaining such data annotations is often very challenging in the predominantly mobile scenarios of Human Activity Recognition. As a result, labels often carry a degree of uncertainty-label jitter-with regards to: i) correct temporal alignments of activity boundaries; and ii) correctness of the actual label provided by the human annotator. In this work, we present a scheme that explicitly incorporates label jitter into the model training process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method through a systematic experimental evaluation on standard recognition tasks for which our method leads to significant increases of mean F1 scores.

Compared to existing methods, we additionally utilize the time-series aspect of HAR. The label noise (or smoothing) at boundaries is inferred from the temporal contexts such as activity transitions and overlaps.

## 3 Effect of Temporal Label Misalignment

As discussed earlier, the standard discrete annotation scheme comes with the challenge for human annotators to identify activity boundaries with sample-by-sample precision. In order to evaluate the sensitivity of conventional HAR systems to label jitter, we evaluate the impact of discrete activity boundary misalignments on model predictive performance. During model training, we shifted existing labels back and forth in time. We then trained a conventional HAR system (details below), and evaluated the model on the test dataset with unmodified annotation. Specifically, we shifted training labels at the start (Figure 1, blue), end (Figure 1, green) and both (Figure 1, red) of boundaries to evaluate the impact of label jitter. The degree of shifts for each boundary was decided proportionally to the length of the activity to account for different activity lengths. For example, the effect of a 1 second boundary shift is different for the activities of either 0.1 seconds duration or lasting 1 minute. For this evaluation, we used the Opportunity dataset [6], and a state-of-the-art ConvLSTM classifier [24], which not only automatically learns the feature representation but also models long-term temporal contexts. We set the maximum percentage of temporal shifts to ±50% on the either side of the boundaries.

Results of this exploration study are summarized in Figure 1 (right). It can be seen that the model performance is very sensitive to all three kinds of boundary shifts. In any case, even missing 0.16 seconds (±5%, 4 ~ 5 samples; 30Hz) led to a statistically significant drop in prediction performance on the test dataset. Interestingly, the performance drop was more severe when underfilling the activity interval, such as, T_p > 0 for start boundary drift, T_p < 0 for end boundary drift, and all T_p for whole interval drift. Thus, to manage boundary uncertainty, the discrete annotation scheme requires annotators to be precise at sample level for the transition point of activity. Yet, activity transitions and overlaps make it ambiguous to draw such hard boundaries.

## 4 Adaptive Smooth Activity Transition

We introduce our approach for directly integrating activity boundary uncertainty into the currently dominating discrete labeling scheme. First of all, uncertainty modeling commonly employs a probabilistic representation [17]. Similarly, we consider the given annotations as a multinomial distribution that associates multiple labels with a degree of confidence [4, 38]. Additionally, the core (middle) interval of an activity typically captures the motions that are specific to an activity class. For such core activities, multiple annotators typically agree in their labelling [37]. Accordingly, we assume that label jitter is unlikely in the core activity.

For boundary annotations, we consider label jitter from two perspectives. First, an activity transition (TR) induces uncertainty at the on-set and off-set boundary between the target activity and NULL (background) interval. For shorter activities, larger portions of an activity belong to this transition interval, which increases the uncertainty of an activity boundaries. Second, more overlapping activities (OV) are observed for shorter NULL intervals between subsequent activities. The short NULL intervals (sub-second level) can merely be an activity transition between those subsequent activities [10]. Such short NULL intervals occur frequently in daily activities. For example, in Table 1 (b) (Opportunity), more than a quarter of NULL intervals are shorter than a second where activities are occurring back-to-back.

Considering these two aspects, our approach infers the distribution of boundary specific label jitter, which increases jointly at a boundary if a target activity has: i) a shorter duration, and thus a more transitional portion in an activity with larger uncertainty; or ii) a shorter null interval between subsequent activities, and thus hence more overlap in activities with larger uncertainty.
